extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers interested in imaginative writing, description, and aesthetic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing descriptive writing and imagery that pleases the imagination, especially visual/landscape description in poetry and prose. Emphasises what qualities of objects and scenes provoke delight and how to shape descriptions to evoke those pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sight as the principal source of imaginative pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our Sight is the most perfect and most delightful of all our Senses. It fills the Mind with the largest Variety of Ideas, converses with its Objects at the greatest Distance, and continues the longest in Action without being tired or satiated with its proper Enjoyments."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise visual imagery in descriptive writing: use objects that can be seen at a distance, provide a variety of visible details, and allow the scene to occupy the reader's attention for sustained pleasure. Treat visual description as the chief vehicle for imaginative delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Pleasures of the Imagination (primary vs secondary)
rubrics_metrics.description: "By the Pleasures of the Imagination ... I here mean such as arise from visible Objects, either when we have them actually in our View, or when we call up their Ideas in our Minds by Paintings, Statues, Descriptions..." (primary = actual view; secondary = ideas/memory/imagined).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both immediate sensory description (primary pleasures) and evocative memory or suggested images (secondary pleasures). Distinguish whether you are depicting a present scene or summoning remembered/fictional images, and exploit each mode's strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness (scale and expansiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure arises from the sight of what is "Great" — not only the bulk of a single object but "the Largeness of a whole View, considered as one entire Piece." Examples: open champaign country, vast deserts, mountains, wide expanses of waters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create or describe expansive vistas and grand scales to induce awe and a 'pleasing Astonishment.' Emphasise horizons, immensity, and the sense of room and liberty in the scene to free the reader's imagination from confinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncommonness / Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything that is "new or uncommon raises a Pleasure in the Imagination, because it fills the Soul with an agreeable Surprize, gratifies its Curiosity..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce unexpected or fresh elements to prevent satiety: surprising details, uncommon sights, shifting phenomena (e.g., waterfalls, meteors). Use novelty to refresh attention and reward curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty (species-specific and formal qualities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty strikes the mind with immediate joy; there is beauty in our own species and a second kind in products of art/nature consisting of "Gaiety or Variety of Colours, in the Symmetry and Proportion of Parts, in the Arrangement and Disposition of Bodies, or in a just Mixture and Concurrence of all together."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ colour, proportion, symmetry, and harmonious arrangements in description. Attend to both instinctive, species-based attractions and the formal qualities of composition (colour, balance, pattern) when creating pleasurable images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination amplifies pleasure (Great, New, Beautiful together)
rubrics_metrics.description: "As the Fancy delights in every thing that is Great, Strange, or Beautiful, and is still more pleased the more it finds of these Perfections in the same Object..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layer qualities — make scenes simultaneously grand, novel, and beautiful. Combining multiple pleasurable principles increases the intensity of the imaginative response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of multiple senses to heighten visual pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: Other senses (sound, smell) heighten the pleasures of the imagination: "Thus any continued Sound... awakens every moment the Mind of the Beholder... If there arises a Fragrancy of Smells or Perfumes, they heighten the Pleasures..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enrich visual description with auditory and olfactory details (birdsong, water noise, perfumes) to intensify the reader's experience and make colours/landscapes seem more vivid and agreeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion sustains attention; static sameness tires
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes that change (rivers, jets d'eau, falls of water) continuously entertain the sight; by contrast, fixed, unchanging landscapes quickly tire the observer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include dynamic elements — movement, flowing water, shifting light — to keep the imagination engaged. Avoid long passages of wholly static description without variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety and contrast prevent satiety
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty and variety relieve the weariness of repeated shows of the same things; "It serves us for a kind of Refreshment, and takes off from that Satiety..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce contrasts and a variety of forms, colours, and positions in a scene. Avoid monotonous repetition; sequence different focal points to refresh the reader's attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer natural grandeur; art succeeds when resembling nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature's works often afford a nobler pleasure than art, but art is most pleasing when it resembles nature: "we find the Works of Nature still more pleasant, the more they resemble those of Art... and artificial Works receive a greater Advantage from their Resemblance of such as are natural."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inventing or describing artificial scenes (gardens, buildings), aim to reproduce the irregularity and scale of nature. Let artful design imitate natural variety rather than imposing excessive neatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive formal regularity in landscape/garden depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of overly trimmed, geometrical gardens: "Our Trees rise in Cones, Globes, and Pyramids. We see the Marks of the Scissars upon every Plant... an Orchard in Flower looks infinitely more delightful, than all the little Labyrinths of the finished Parterre."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor organic, irregular detail over artificial over-ordering in descriptive portrayal of gardens and vegetation. Convey the sense of uncontrived life rather than visible manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture: consider both bulk and manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness in architecture may relate to the bulk of the structure or the manner in which it is built; grandeur of construction contributes to imaginative pleasure (example references to ancient large works).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing buildings, attend to both scale and the manner/technique of construction. Emphasise vastness, boldness, and distinctive methods to evoke awe and imaginative interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate the 'polite imagination'—retain, alter, and compound images
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Man of a Polite Imagination' can 'converse with a Picture' and 'retain, alter and compound' images to form agreeable visions; the imagination makes even a dungeon bearable by creating beautiful landskips in the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write in ways that invite readers to manipulate and dwell on images: provide suggestive, combinable details that allow the reader's imagination to compose richer visions than explicit description alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance awe with potential disgust (manage mixture of horror)
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be something 'so terrible or offensive, that the Horror or Loathsomeness of an Object may over-bear the Pleasure which results from its Greatness, Novelty, or Beauty; but still there will be such a Mixture of Delight in the very Disgust...'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that grotesque or horrific elements can both contribute to and overwhelm pleasure; use them intentionally and balance with other pleasurable qualities to preserve rather than extinguish imaginative delight.
